title: What hearing conservation training does OSHA require every year?
description: OSHA 1910.95(k) hearing conservation training: who is covered at 85 dBA, annual repetition, the three required topics and access duties, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) occupational noise standard, 29 CFR 1910.95(k), requires employers to train every employee exposed to noise at or above an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels and to repeat that training annually. Training must cover the effects of noise on hearing, hearing protectors, and audiometric testing. Paragraph (l) adds access duties: a copy of the standard posted in the workplace and training materials supplied to OSHA on request.
keyTakeaways: The trigger is the action level: an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels, or a dose of fifty percent, measured without regard to hearing protection, under 1910.95(c).
Training is annual for everyone in the hearing conservation program under 1910.95(k)(2), and its content must be updated when protective equipment or work processes change.

Paragraph (k)(3) fixes three topics: effects of noise on hearing; hearing protector purpose, types, attenuation, selection, fitting, use and care; and the purpose and procedure of audiometric testing.
A standard threshold shift on an annual audiogram triggers fitting, training, or refitting and retraining in hearing protector use under 1910.95(g)(8).
Paragraph (l) requires the standard to be posted and made available, and all training materials to be provided to OSHA on request.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry employers with employees exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA, such as manufacturing, food processing, printing, woodworking and metal fabrication
Employees included in the hearing conservation program
Audiometric technicians and the professionals who review audiograms
Not employers engaged in oil and gas well drilling and servicing operations, which paragraph (o) exempts from paragraphs (c) through (n)

sections.heading: Who must receive hearing conservation training?

blocks.text: Every employee exposed to noise at or above an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) of 85 decibels on the A scale must be trained. Paragraph (c)(1) of [29 CFR 1910.95](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.95) requires a "continuing, effective hearing conservation program" whenever exposures equal or exceed that level, or equivalently a dose of fifty percent, and paragraph (c)(2) names this the action level. Exposure is computed without regard to any attenuation from hearing protectors, so wearing earplugs does not take an employee out of the program.

Paragraph (k)(1) then requires the employer to train each employee exposed at or above the action level, to institute a training program, and to ensure employee participation. Coverage depends on monitoring results under paragraph (d), which requires a monitoring program when information indicates any employee may reach 85 dBA, with a sampling strategy designed to identify employees for inclusion in the program. OSHA's [noise topic page](https://www.osha.gov/noise) confirms that the program requirement applies to general industry, maritime and longshoring worksites.

sections.heading: What must the annual training cover?

blocks.text: Paragraph (k)(3) requires the employer to ensure that each employee is informed of three topics. They are narrow but specific, and each maps directly to another part of the program:

items: The effects of noise on hearing.
The purpose of hearing protectors, the advantages, disadvantages and attenuation of various types, and instructions on selection, fitting, use and care.
The purpose of audiometric testing, and an explanation of the test procedures.

blocks.text: The second topic connects to paragraph (i)(3), which gives employees the opportunity to select their hearing protectors from a variety of suitable protectors, and to paragraph (i)(5), which requires the employer to ensure proper initial fitting and supervise correct use. The third topic connects to paragraph (g), which requires a baseline audiogram within 6 months of first exposure at or above the action level (1 year where mobile test vans are used) and an annual audiogram after that. Training that explains the 14-hour quiet period before a baseline test, required by (g)(5)(iii), makes the test results more reliable.

sections.heading: How often must hearing conservation training be repeated?

blocks.text: The training must be repeated annually for each employee in the program. Paragraph (k)(2) says the program "shall be repeated annually for each employee included in the hearing conservation program" and that the information "shall be updated to be consistent with changes in protective equipment and work processes."

Two further events create training duties outside the annual cycle. If an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift, defined in (g)(10) as an average change of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear, paragraph (g)(8)(ii) requires that employees not using hearing protectors be fitted, trained in their use and care, and required to use them, and that employees already using protectors be refitted and retrained. The employee must be told of the shift in writing within 21 days of the determination under (g)(8)(i). Paragraph (i)(4) separately requires training in the use and care of all hearing protectors provided.

blocks.title: Practical scheduling point
blocks.text: Many employers deliver the annual (k) training on the day of the annual audiogram. That keeps the two annual cycles aligned, gives a natural point to refit protectors, and means a threshold shift found that day can be followed by documented retraining.

sections.heading: What does paragraph (l) require on access to information?

blocks.text: Paragraph (l) requires three things. Under (l)(1) the employer must make copies of the standard available to affected employees or their representatives and post a copy in the workplace. Under (l)(2) it must provide affected employees with any informational materials about the standard supplied by the Assistant Secretary. Under (l)(3) it must provide, upon request, all materials related to its training and education program under the standard to the Assistant Secretary and the Director.

Paragraph (l)(3) is the practical evidence duty. The noise standard does not prescribe a training record, and the recordkeeping paragraph (m) lists only exposure measurements and audiometric test records. Noise exposure measurement records must be kept for two years and audiometric test records for the duration of the affected employee's employment under (m)(3). An employer that cannot produce its slide deck, handouts and attendance for the annual cycle will struggle to show that (k) was met, even though no specific form is required.

sections.heading: What evidence shows a compliant hearing conservation training program?

blocks.text: An auditor will try to trace each employee on the noise exposure roster to an annual training event, an annual audiogram, and a fitted protector. The table maps each paragraph to the person it applies to, its timing and the evidence expected.

sections.heading: How should employers build hearing conservation training?

blocks.text: Start from the monitoring data, because program membership defines the training population. Repeat monitoring is required under (d)(3) whenever a change in production, process, equipment or controls increases noise exposures to the extent that additional employees may be exposed at or above the action level or protectors may be rendered inadequate. Each repeat survey should therefore update the training roster as well as the protector selection.

Treat the protector types actually stocked as the training content, since (k)(2) ties updates to changes in protective equipment. A change of earplug model is both a procurement event and a training event. The same logic applies across OSHA standards with annual cycles; see [OSHA respiratory protection training](/regulations/osha-respiratory-protection-training-requirements) for a parallel structure and [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) for the overview. For scheduling annual cycles, see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles), and for a site level view see [how to build a training matrix for a manufacturing plant](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-manufacturing-plant).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the three (k)(3) topics as separate assessment points and links each hearing protector model to the training content that describes it. When a monitoring survey or a protector change is recorded, the affected employees and the content that needs revision are identified together.

faqs.q: Do employees who always wear earplugs still need hearing conservation training?
faqs.a: Yes. Paragraph (c)(1) computes exposure without regard to the attenuation provided by personal protective equipment. An employee whose unprotected exposure reaches an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA is in the program and must be trained annually, whatever protectors they wear.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require a written training record for hearing conservation?
faqs.a: No specific record is prescribed. Paragraph (m) covers exposure measurements and audiograms only. However, paragraph (l)(3) requires the employer to provide all training materials to OSHA on request, so dated attendance and content records are the practical way to show the annual training happened.

faqs.q: Does the hearing conservation training requirement apply to construction?
faqs.a: The 1910.95 hearing conservation program, including paragraph (k), is a general industry provision. OSHA's noise topic page describes the program requirement as applying to general industry, maritime and longshoring worksites. Paragraph (o) also exempts oil and gas well drilling and servicing operations.

faqs.q: Can hearing conservation training be done online?
faqs.a: The standard requires employees to be informed of three topics and does not specify a delivery method. Fitting and correct use of protectors, however, must be ensured and supervised under paragraph (i)(5), which usually needs an in-person element alongside any online content.

factCheck.claim: 1910.95(c)(1)-(2): continuing, effective hearing conservation program at or above 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA or dose of fifty percent, computed without regard to PPE attenuation; this is the action level.
1910.95(k)(1)-(3): train each employee at or above 85 dBA TWA; repeat annually; update for changes in protective equipment and work processes; three topics listed.
1910.95(l)(1)-(3): copies of standard available and posted; OSHA informational materials provided; all training materials provided upon request to the Assistant Secretary and the Director.

1910.95(g)(5): baseline audiogram within 6 months of first exposure (1 year with mobile vans), preceded by 14 hours without workplace noise; (g)(6) annual audiogram; (g)(10) standard threshold shift is average 10 dB at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz.
1910.95(g)(8): written notice of STS within 21 days; employees fitted and trained, or refitted and retrained, in hearing protector use.
1910.95(i)(3)-(5): choice of protectors, training in use and care, proper initial fitting and supervised use; (d)(3) repeat monitoring on changes.
1910.95(m)(3): noise exposure records kept two years, audiometric records for duration of employment; (o) exempts oil and gas well drilling and servicing from (c) through (n).
OSHA noise page: hearing conservation program required at general industry, maritime and longshoring worksites when exposures equal or exceed 85 dBA TWA.
